record.paper_title: Anomalous transport in the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model: a review and open problems
record.original_question: When conservative stochastic momentum-exchange noise is added to a nonlinear Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou chain, why can the observed finite-size scaling appear to move toward different effective exponents even though the asymptotic universality class is argued to remain unchanged? Equivalently, what mechanism lets conservative noise alter convergence rates and effective thermal resistance without changing the long-distance hydrodynamic universality class?

evidence.quote: it is unclear the reason why the scaling behavior should be accelerated by the addition of an extra conservative noise, which, a priori, should more reasonably lower the conductivity (increase the thermal resistance).
conservative noise does not change the universality class.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator chain of N sites with Hamiltonian
  H = Σ_i [ p_i^2/(2m) + V(q_{i+1} - q_i) ],
where V is a nonlinear nearest-neighbor interaction potential (for instance the Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou potential V(r) = (1/2)r^2 + (α/3)r^3 + (β/4)r^4, with α ≥ 0 and β > 0). The chain is coupled at its two ends to Langevin heat baths at temperatures T_L and T_R, and after a long time it reaches a nonequilibrium stationary state with a heat current J(N) and an effective finite-size thermal conductivity
  κ(N) = J(N) N / (T_L − T_R).
For nonintegrable potentials, κ(N) is expected to diverge as κ(N) ∼ N^δ for large N, with the exponent δ determined by a hydrodynamic universality class (δ = 1/3 for asymmetric potentials in the KPZ class, δ = 1/2 for symmetric potentials).

Now superimpose on the deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics a "conservative" stochastic noise that, at independent random times, exchanges the momenta of randomly chosen neighboring particles (or, more generally, applies random rotations to neighboring momentum pairs). This noise preserves total momentum and total kinetic energy at every event, and in the limit where it dominates one obtains a stochastic system whose hydrodynamic universality class for energy transport is rigorously known and is argued to coincide with that of the purely deterministic chain.

Problem. Provide a quantitative explanation of the following empirical observation. When the conservative momentum-exchange noise is added to the FPUT chain, the apparent finite-size exponent δ_eff(N) extracted from κ(N) ∼ N^{δ_eff(N)} on accessible system sizes can shift toward values different from (and in particular larger than) the deterministic one, even though the asymptotic universality class is unchanged. Specifically:

(a) Identify the mechanism by which adding a conservative noise — which on physical grounds should reduce the conductivity by introducing additional momentum scrambling — instead accelerates the apparent convergence of κ(N) and modifies its effective growth exponent at finite N.

(b) Derive (or characterize) how the crossover length N* separating the preasymptotic regime from the true asymptotic anomalous regime depends on the noise rate γ, and explain why N* can decrease with γ even when the long-wavelength hydrodynamic exponent δ does not depend on γ.

(c) Reconcile (a) and (b) with the statement that the conservative noise leaves the long-distance hydrodynamic universality class invariant.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of why a conservative momentum-exchange noise accelerates finite-size scaling and shifts the apparent conductivity exponent in FPUT chains, while not changing the asymptotic hydrodynamic universality class, is highlighted as an unresolved issue in the recent review on anomalous transport in FPUT and remains discussed in the literature without a generally accepted quantitative explanation. Related work has clarified universality classes (KPZ δ=1/3 vs. symmetric δ=1/2) and the role of finite-size crossovers, but no source verified here provides a definitive resolution of the mechanism.

status_evidence.snippet: Listed among open problems on conservative noise mechanisms affecting finite-size scaling without changing universality class.
status_evidence.claim: The mechanism is explicitly listed as an open problem in the review.

status_evidence.title: A violation of universality in anomalous Fourier's law
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses subtleties and apparent violations in the universal exponents for anomalous heat conduction in 1D chains.
status_evidence.claim: Effective finite-size exponents in 1D anomalous transport remain debated.

status_evidence.title: Anomalous Energy Transport in FPU-β Chain
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews δ=1/3 vs δ=1/2 scenarios and finite-size crossovers in FPU chains with and without noise.
status_evidence.claim: Universality class is robust but finite-size exponents differ; mechanism not fully explained.
